title: Better analytical ideas, made tangible.
section: Faster implementation changes more than speed.
text:
Faster implementation changes more than speed.
AI-assisted development can reduce the distance between a well-reasoned healthcare problem and a working analytical system. More importantly, lower implementation cost expands the set of solutions worth considering before one structure becomes expensive to replace.

The goal is not maximum sophistication. It is less compromise for the wrong reasons. Statistical reasoning, domain expertise, validation, and judgment still determine what should be built.

title: Better analytical ideas, made tangible.
text:
Structure Before Sophistication
Sophisticated-looking outputs are becoming easier to generate. Understanding the healthcare problem, defining what should be measured, making assumptions explicit, and determining how the work will be used are not.
Expanded technical capability does not make complexity inherently better. A simple method is still the right method when it matches the question, data, and decision. Get the structure right first, then add complexity only where it improves the solution.


Clear questionsStart with the healthcare question and the decision it needs to support.


Defensible logicMake definitions, metrics, assumptions, and analytical choices open to review.


Reproducible systemsBuild work that can be understood, repeated, and maintained.


Honest boundariesMake uncertainty, limitations, and appropriate use part of the system.

title: Bring structure to difficult analytical problems.
text:
Structure Before Sophistication
Most analytical problems do not begin with dashboards or models. They begin with questions. CentralStatz works through the structure behind the problem before building a solution.
It is easy to focus on the output first. But the output is only as useful as the reasoning and processes behind it: clear definitions, reproducible workflows, defensible metrics, and maintainable implementation.


Clear questionsDefine what the work is meant to answer and support.


Defensible logicMake measures and assumptions open to review.


Reproducible systemsBuild work that can be understood, repeated, and maintained.


Appropriate toolsUse sophistication only where the problem earns it.

Meet Alex Zajichek
Alex is a statistician and data scientist in Central Wisconsin with more than a decade of experience working across healthcare research, analytics, and data science.
His work is especially grounded in healthcare, where messy systems, consequential decisions, and fragile metrics make sound analytical structure essential. Through CentralStatz, he helps teams and organizations build reproducible analytics, strengthen statistical reasoning, and create systems and processes that make complex questions easier to answer over time.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
text:
Why this exists
Hospitals may have a readmission score when a patient leaves, but that score cannot show what happens next. Time passes, new information arrives, and some patients are readmitted or die. A care team needs to know what the remaining risk looks like now, not only what it looked like at discharge.
The information is often fragmented, too. People doing follow-up may see one picture, analysts another, and quality or executive leaders a third. The long-term idea behind Readmission Risk Pool (RRP) is to connect those views so decisions about individual patients and the hospital-wide picture can be understood together.
I began exploring that idea several years ago. The original 2024 article explains the practical problem that started it.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
text:
What is available today
RRP is now implemented and distributed as the open-source readmit R package. Version 1.0.0 is the first major public release. Its package website is the main place for setup instructions, the application preview, a simulated-hospital walkthrough, and technical reference material.
With readmit, an analyst or developer can create an ordinary project owned by their organization. The project includes places to connect local source data, provide a local risk method, and customize its Shiny application. At chosen times after discharge, RRP assesses eligible patients, saves the results, and prepares views of current remaining risk, recorded changes in risk, and a summary of the assessment.
This is a working analytical foundation. The supplied application lets a user explore the risk pool and recorded trajectories. It is not yet a care-management task list or a hospital executive reporting system; those broader uses remain questions for practical testing and local implementation.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
text:
A changing question, asked consistently
For a patient still in the 30-day follow-up period who has not had a known readmission or death, each assessment asks: What is the remaining chance of a first readmission before 30 days have elapsed since the original discharge?
Another assessment does not start a new 30-day clock. It uses information available at that assessment time and records the answer as it stood then. That matters when a new event becomes known later: the earlier assessment remains part of the history rather than being silently rewritten.
RRP supplies this shared question and the rules for who is eligible. The organization supplies the model or other method for producing the estimate. Different hospitals can use methods suited to their own data and patients without changing what the resulting probability means.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
text:
From package to local project
The path is intentionally small enough to inspect before an organization commits to a larger implementation:

Install readmit from CRAN and create a project. The package gives the team an editable starting structure, including the application. The data and risk scripts begin as stubs; they do not pretend to be a working hospital model.
Connect approved hospital data. The organization maps its discharge and event information into RRP’s shared structure, keeping source-system details under local control.
Supply and evaluate a risk method. The local method estimates the remaining chance of readmission for eligible patients. The package does not provide a clinically validated model.
Assess, refresh, and explore. Run assessments at chosen times, inspect the retained history, then refresh the application’s views. The app reads those results; opening it does not calculate a new risk estimate.

The getting-started guide and simulated-hospital walkthrough show the full path without requiring a hospital data connection.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
section: What the current views can and cannot say
text:
What the current views can and cannot say
The application presents the latest accepted risk estimates for eligible episodes and the estimates actually recorded for a selected episode over time. An operational summary accounts for the episodes assessed, including those with a known readmission, death, closed follow-up window, or a risk calculation that could not be completed.
That makes the analytical history inspectable. It does not by itself tell a care team whom to contact, what intervention to choose, or whether acting on a prediction will improve outcomes. Those decisions need local clinical judgment, workflow design, model evaluation, and governance.
The diagram above illustrates how current analytical views could eventually connect daily follow-up with leadership oversight. The RRP website shows an actual application screenshot using simulated data and explains the current product in more detail.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
text:
Open source, locally owned
readmit is free to install from CRAN and is released under the Apache-2.0 license. The organization owns its project, data connections, risk method, and application changes. The package provides a common analytical structure, while the hospital remains responsible for privacy, security, clinical validation, monitoring, and appropriate use.
The first release makes the idea available for hands-on evaluation. It is not evidence that a model is accurate for a particular hospital or that the platform has improved patient outcomes.
